name: Lena Novak

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Lena. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Does that sound all right?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Yes, that's fine. I'm not much of a talker about this stuff, but I'll be honest with you.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work for Brennan Electrical, a four-person firm in an old mill town, mostly rewiring terraced houses that haven't been touched since the seventies. Mick Brennan, the owner, sends me in first to lift floorboards and chase walls, then I run cable and he checks everything before it's live. I love the moment a dead house comes back on and the owner flicks a switch. What wears me out is the dust, the cold lofts, and the fact I still freeze when Mick asks me a question about the regulations.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Here's the card: "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly hype. Okay. That one sounds like what the old lads at the wholesaler say already.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, honestly. At the union branch meeting I'd say the robots never came and we still need proper wages and proper training. I don't post online much, but I'd share something like that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, nothing changing isn't great either. Rent on our flat went up twice this year, Mick's had two quiet weeks this autumn, and there are maybe three firms in town that take on juniors. I've got about 300 in the bank, which doesn't even cover a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my head down and keep turning up at seven for Mick. I'd go to every union branch meeting, because the pay rise for juniors is the thing that would actually help. I'd also try to do the next part of my licence course at night, though I keep putting it off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tired, mostly. It's a relief that no machine is coming for me, but I'm still one bad month away from asking my mum for rent money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said Mick's had quiet weeks. What happens to you in a quiet week?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He sends me home early and I lose the hours, because I'm paid by the hour. A quiet week at work means the gas bill goes on a card. No robot did that to me, a slow autumn did. Sam, my partner, picked up an extra night shift at the care home to cover it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why do you keep putting the licence course off?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's 40 evenings and it costs more than I've got, and I'm wrecked by six. Part of it is I'm scared I'll fail the exam, because I'm slower than the other juniors on the theory. Nobody in my family has done exams since school.

say: I'd tell the union branch the **robots never came** and juniors still need fair pay.
I'd say the old electricians were right that **AI was hype**.
think: Nothing changing still leaves me with a **thin cushion** and rising rent.
With only three local firms hiring juniors, **quiet weeks** at Brennan's scare me more than AI.
do: Keep turning up at **seven** for Mick and take every hour offered.
Attend every **union branch** meeting to push for a junior pay rise.
Try to start the **licence course** at night, though the 40 evenings cost too much.
feel: Relieved that **no machine** is coming, but **tired** of living one bad month from borrowing.
S0.quote: A quiet week at work means the gas bill goes on a card. No robot did that to me, a slow autumn did.
fieldNote: Her worry here has nothing to do with **AI**: hourly pay and quiet weeks drive it.
She defers the **licence course** out of cost and fear of exams, not lack of interest.
Her partner's **extra night shift** is the household's real safety net.

steps.text: Take every hour Mick offers at Brennan Electrical
Go to the monthly union branch meeting about junior pay

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Thinking tasks first, robots slower. So the paperwork side goes before the hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly why we need the union and rules on how firms use it. I'd say it at the branch and probably in the van to Mick. Software shouldn't be an excuse to stop training juniors.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I don't do the thinking bits anyway, Mick does the quotes and the certificates. If software does those, Mick might not need to pay for an office morning, but he'd still need someone to lift floorboards. Software can do my boss's paperwork, fine. The real worry is my boss doing the sums and deciding one old hand with an app beats paying a slow junior.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Mick straight out whether he's planning to cut hours. I'd put 20 a week aside, even if it means no takeaways, so I've got some cushion. I won't touch the apps myself, but I'd go to whatever the union runs on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy at first, then a knot in my stomach when I think of Mick doing his sums.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you won't touch the apps. Even if Mick asked you to?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If Mick made me, I'd do it, but badly. I'm not good on screens and I don't trust them to tell me what's safe. Electrics kill people if you get them wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about at work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Me, honestly, then Dean, the other junior, because he's even newer. The older two are fine, they know everything. It's always the bottom rung that goes.

say: I'd say this is why the **union** and **rules on AI** matter.
I'd argue software shouldn't become an excuse to **stop training juniors**.
think: The **quotes and certificates** are Mick's job, so software doesn't touch my tasks directly.
My fear is Mick deciding one experienced electrician plus an **app** beats keeping me.
do: Ask Mick **straight out** whether he plans to cut my hours.
Put **20 a week** aside by cutting takeaways.
Go to any **union session** on AI, but avoid the apps myself.
feel: **Uneasy**, with a **knot** in my stomach when I picture Mick doing his sums.
S1.quote: Software can do my boss's paperwork, fine. The real worry is my boss doing the sums and deciding one old hand with an app beats paying a slow junior.
fieldNote: She sees the **indirect threat**: AI cuts the boss's costs, making a junior easier to drop.
She would use AI **only under orders**, and mainly distrusts it on **safety**.
She frames the bottom rung as **always first to go**.

steps.text: Put 20 a week into savings instead of takeaways
Attend the union's session on AI at work

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's nothing. I'd still be a junior in 2028.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say governments let tech firms run wild and now ordinary people pay. I'd be at any march the union called. I'd say it loudly, which isn't like me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd be finished by 2031 when the robots come, and maybe sooner. The thinking side going in 2028 means Mick's quoting and design are free, so the only thing left to sell is hands, and robot hands come three years later. I'd be 32 with no licence, no savings and no other trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sign up for whatever government support exists, straight away, before the queue gets long. I'd go to the union's meetings and any protest about a robot tax or wage support. I honestly don't know what else, because I can't afford a course and I wouldn't know which course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick. Like the floor's gone. I don't have a plan and I don't have the money to make one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Sam that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we might have to move back to my mum's for a while. Sam would say it's fine, because that's Sam, but my mum's place is a two-bed with my brother still in it. I'd probably cry in the bathroom so Sam didn't see.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's Sam's job like in that picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Care work is hands-on too, so maybe it lasts until the robots, same as mine. My partner and I both do hands-on work, so we'd both fall off the same cliff in the same year. That's the bit that makes me feel sick.

say: I'd say governments let **tech firms run wild** and workers pay the price.
I'd join any **union march** for a robot tax or wage support.
think: With AGI in 2028, Mick's **quoting is free** and only hands are left to sell.
When robots arrive in **2031**, I'd be 32 with no licence and no savings.
Sam's **care work** and my wiring could both go in the same year.
do: Apply for **government support** straight away, before the queue gets long.
Attend **union meetings** and protests about a robot tax.
Prepare to move back to **my mum's** two-bed with my brother.
feel: Sick, like the **floor's gone**, with **no plan** and no money to make one.
S2.quote: My partner and I both do hands-on work, so we'd both fall off the same cliff in the same year.
fieldNote: The **two-person household** both in hands-on work doubles her exposure in 2031.
She says outright she has **no plan** and no means to make one.
Her public anger is louder than usual, but **privately she freezes**.

steps.text: Apply for government income support as soon as AGI lands
Join the union march for wage support
Back the campaign for a tax on robot labour
Move back into Mum's two-bed flat with Sam if needed

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years, robots in 2034. That's a bit better than the last one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got five years, so let's use them, and I'd mean the government. I'd say it at the branch: get training paid for now, not after. Online I'd share the union's stuff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years is enough for me to get my licence if I stop making excuses. Robots come in 2034, so I'd have seven years of hands-on work left, which is time to save a bit. But a licensed electrician in 2034 still faces robots, so it only buys time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the licence course next September, and I'd ask the union if there's a fund to pay for it. I'd save 30 a week once I'm qualified and earning more. I'd push for the union to get juniors guaranteed apprenticeships before the robots arrive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, but less frozen than with two years. At least there's a ladder to climb, even if it leads somewhere that's also going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd stop making excuses. What's the real excuse?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fear, mainly. I failed my maths resit at school and I still feel thick in a classroom. Mick says I'm good with my hands, I'm just slow on the paper side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When the thinking AI arrives in 2031, what would change in your day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mick would quote on his phone and the testing paperwork would fill itself in. AI doing the testing paperwork actually helps a slow junior like me for three years. Then the robots come for the part I'm good at.

say: I'd say we have **five years**, so the government should fund training **now**.
I'd share the **union's** posts calling for guaranteed apprenticeships.
think: Five years is enough to get my **licence** if I stop making excuses.
Robots in **2034** leave me seven years of work, which **buys time** but doesn't save me.
do: Start the **licence course** next September with union funding if possible.
Save **30 a week** once qualified and earning more.
Push the union for **guaranteed apprenticeships** for juniors.
feel: **Scared** but less frozen, because there's a **ladder** to climb.
S3.quote: AI doing the testing paperwork actually helps a slow junior like me for three years. Then the robots come for the part I'm good at.
fieldNote: She spots a **twist**: thinking AI covers her weak spot, paperwork, before robots arrive.
Her barrier to the licence is **fear of exams**, rooted in school.
Five years moves her from frozen to **reluctant planning**.

steps.text: Enrol in the electrician's licence course next September
Lobby the union branch for guaranteed junior apprenticeships

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. 2039 for the robots. I'd be nearly 40.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade is plenty of time if governments actually act, so no excuses. I'd say that at the branch and to anyone who'd listen. Workers should get a share of what robots earn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years means I could get licensed, get good, and maybe move to the inspection or maintenance side that robots reach last. Mick will retire before then, so I'd have to find another firm anyway. Still, I'd only be early forties when it all lands, with no savings to speak of unless something changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the licence course over the next two years, then ask Mick to teach me inspection and testing. I'd keep going to the union and get onto the branch committee, because I want a say. Sam and I would try to put something aside every month, even 50.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but it's a normal sort of anxious. Ten years of warning is like knowing your boiler dies in ten years. You can plan for it, as long as you're not skint.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said 'if you're not skint'. Are you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. Right now I am, and that's the part AI doesn't fix. If I'm still on junior pay at 30, ten years doesn't help much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a 16-year-old thinking of becoming an electrician?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell a 16-year-old to do it, but to get the licence fast and learn the inspection side. And to join the union on day one, because nobody else looks out for you.

say: I'd say a decade is **plenty of time** if governments actually act.
I'd argue workers deserve a **share of robot earnings**.
think: Ten years lets me **get licensed** and move into **inspection** work robots reach last.
If I'm still on **junior pay** at 30, the extra time helps little.
do: Finish the **licence course** within two years.
Ask Mick to teach me **inspection and testing**.
Stand for the union **branch committee** and save **50** a month with Sam.
feel: **Anxious**, but a normal kind you can **plan around**, like an old boiler.
S4.quote: Ten years of warning is like knowing your boiler dies in ten years. You can plan for it, as long as you're not skint.
fieldNote: The decade lets her picture a **career path**, which the shorter scenarios did not.
Low pay, not AI, remains her **core problem**.
Her advice to a teenager shows she still **values the trade**.

steps.text: Complete the licence course within two years
Learn inspection and testing from Mick
Stand for the union branch committee

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, no question, because Sam and I would both be out within a few years and I've got nothing saved. What would help is the government paying for training and a wage while you retrain, and a proper junior pay rise now so I can actually build a cushion.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the partners. Everyone asks what happens to me, but Sam is my partner and we split everything. Nobody plans for two people losing hands-on work at once. My rent depends on my partner's shifts as much as mine.

headlineQuote: Nobody plans for two people losing hands-on work at once. My rent depends on my partner's shifts as much as mine.
portrait: Lena is a **27-year-old junior** at a small rewiring firm, paid by the hour with under a month saved.
She distrusts **AI tools** and screens, and fears exams after failing maths at school.
Her worry in calm scenarios comes from **quiet weeks** and rising rent, not technology.
With AGI by 2028 she **panics**, because she and partner Sam both do hands-on work.
Longer warnings let her plan a **licence** and inspection work, backed by her **union**.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because she and Sam could both lose hands-on work within a few years.
whatWouldHelp: **Government-paid training** with a wage while retraining.
A **junior pay rise** now so she can build savings.
